title: Custom Packaging Proofs Explained: PDF vs. Physical Structural Samples for Print Accuracy
author: Henry
summary: Vegetable-based inks in box printing utilize bio-based carriers—such as soybean, linseed, canola, or tung oil—to drastically reduce Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) to under $60\text{ g/L}$, while delivering superior pigment saturation, neutral scent profiles, and enhanced paperboard de-inking efficiency during recycling. By swapping out volatile crude-oil distillates for renewable plant oils, custom packaging converters can achieve rich Pantone color matching without sacrificing pressroom safety or environmental compliance. PETROLEUM VS. VEGETABLE INK DYNAMICS PETROLEUM-BASED INK VEGETABLE-BASED INK +----------------------------------+ +----------------------------------+ | Mineral Distillates (Crude Oil) | | Bio-Based Plant Oils (Soy/Flax) | | High VOCs: 250 - 350 g/L | | Low VOCs: 15 - 60 g/L | | Murky, Yellowish Carrier Base | | Crystal-Clear Translucent Base | | Tough, Plasticized Fiber Bond | | Clean Flotation De-Inking | +----------------------------------+ +----------------------------------+ For decades, commercial sheetfed offset and flexographic box printing relied heavily on mineral-oil-derived solvents. These petroleum carriers allowed press operators to run high-speed jobs with fast evaporative flash-off times, but the environmental and physical trade-offs were severe. Petroleum inks off-gas heavy, toxic solvents into pressrooms, leave a pungent chemical odor inside unboxing packages, and fuse tightly to paperboard pulp—making repulping and municipal recycling significantly harder. As global supply chains face mounting regulatory pressure from the EU Green Claims Directive, FTC Green Guides, and corporate ESG mandates, packaging directors are pivoting toward sustainable ink formulations. Moving away from petroleum-based chemistries is no longer just a marketing play; it is an industrial upgrade in print quality and repulpability. This technical guide breaks down the chemical carrier mechanics, optical density advantages, de-inking efficiency, brand benchmarks, and a 5-step procurement framework for transitioning your custom box runs to vegetable-based inks. 1. The Chemistry of Vegetable Inks: How Bio-Based Carriers Replace Petroleum Solvents Understanding how vegetable-based inks function on press requires looking under the hood at ink chemistry. Traditional printing inks rely on three core components: a pigment for color, resins to bind the pigment to the substrate, and a liquid vehicle (carrier) to transport the pigment through the ink rollers onto the printing plate. ANATOMY OF A VEGETABLE-BASED INK +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | BIO-BASED VEHICLE / CARRIER (20% - 40%) | | Derived from Soybean, Linseed, Canola, Tall, or Tung Oils | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | RESINS & BINDERS (30% - 50%) | | Plant-Derived Rosin Esters & Synthetic Binding Polymers | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | PIGMENT & PERFORMANCE ADDITIVES (20% - 30%) | | Organic Colorants, Wax Compounds, & Eco-Friendly Metal Driers | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ The Bio-Based Carrier Vehicle In conventional inks, the liquid vehicle is composed of petroleum distillates—crude oil fractions containing complex volatile hydrocarbons. In vegetable ink formulations, these synthetic solvents are replaced with refined vegetable oils: Soybean Oil: The industry standard for offset box printing due to its stability, low cost, and clear carrier profile. Linseed (Flaxseed) Oil: Known for higher drying speeds and natural film-forming properties via cross-linking oxidation. Canola & Tall Oils: Frequently blended to optimize viscosity and tack ratings across high-speed press rollers. Tung Oil: Used in premium specialty inks to enhance rub resistance and surface hardness. Volatile Organic Compound (VOC) Emission Metrics The primary environmental metric separating ink formulations is the release of Volatile Organic Compounds—carbon-based chemicals that evaporate easily at room temperature, contributing to ground-level ozone, smog, and indoor air pollution. $$\text{VOC Reduction Percentage} = \left( 1 - \frac{30\text{ g/L (Vegetable Avg)}}{300\text{ g/L (Petroleum Avg)}} \right) \times 100 = 90\% \text{ Emission Drop}$$ VOC EMISSIONS BY INK SYSTEM (g/L) PETROLEUM-BASED [====================================] 250 - 350 g/L VEGETABLE-BASED [===] 15 - 60 g/L WATER-BASED [==] 0 - 20 g/L Petroleum-based offset inks typically generate $250\text{ to }350\text{ g/L}$ of VOC emissions as their mineral solvents flash off during setting. In contrast, bio-based vegetable inks release only $15\text{ to }60\text{ g/L}$ —representing an $80\%\text{ to }95\%$ drop in volatile emissions. This massive reduction allows commercial packaging converters to operate well within strict Air Quality Management District (AQMD) regional limits without requiring expensive pressroom catalytic oxidizers. Odor Neutrality & Low-Migration Safety Because mineral oil solvents do not fully evaporate, residual hydrocarbons remain trapped within the printed paperboard matrix. When custom mailer boxes, folding cartons, or rigid presentation boxes are closed, these compounds off-gas into the enclosed headspace. Upon unboxing, consumers are hit with a sharp, industrial chemical odor. Vegetable oils have virtually zero volatility at ambient temperatures. Once cured, they exhibit a neutral scent profile that prevents odor transfer into sensitive contents. This makes bio-based inks essential for direct-to-consumer apparel, cosmetics, subscription boxes, and food-grade packaging operating under strict FDA low-migration rules. 2. Print Quality & De-Inking Mechanics: Vibrancy, Saturation, and Recycling A common misconception among procurement teams is that eco-friendly inks require compromising on visual pop or press speeds. In reality, vegetable carriers offer distinct optical and physical advantages during both the printing process and the post-consumer recycling cycle. OPTICAL LIGHT REFLECTION PETROLEUM CARRIER (Murky/Yellow) VEGETABLE CARRIER (Translucent) | | v v [ Absorbs & Distorts Light ] [ Direct Light Pass-Through ] | | v v Duller Tones / Heavy Pigment Vibrant Pantone Blacks & Solids Optical Clarity & Color Saturation Petroleum distillates are inherently yellowish-brown and murky in their unpigmented state. To achieve true, punchy colors on paperboard, ink chemists must heavily load the formula with pigments to mask the carrier's natural tint. Vegetable oils—especially refined soy and linseed oils—are naturally clear and translucent. When blended with organic pigments: Light passes cleanly through the ink film to reflect off the paperboard surface without color distortion. The ink achieves higher optical density using lower total pigment volumes. Dark Pantone solids, deep rich blacks, and vibrant spot colors display crisp saturation on both coated Solid Bleached Sulfate (SBS) and raw, porous uncoated Kraft stock. Flotation De-Inking & Fiber Retention The true test of a packaging material's circularity occurs at the municipal paper mill during the repulping phase. To recycle printed paperboard into high-grade white paper or virgin-equivalent board, the cured ink must be separated from the wood pulp through a process known as flotation de-inking . FLOTATION DE-INKING MECHANICS PETROLEUM INK ON PULP VEGETABLE INK ON PULP +---------------------------+ +---------------------------+ | - Hard plasticized film | | - Naturally saponifies | | - Fuses to wood fibers | VS. | in alkaline wash | | - Requires harsh bleaches | | - Detaches cleanly | | - Low fiber yield/purity | | - Floats off easily | +---------------------------+ +---------------------------+ Petroleum Inks: Under heat and pressure, mineral oils form hard, plasticized films that grip the cellulosic wood fibers like acrylic paint. Breaking these bonds requires aggressive chemical surfactants and peroxide bleaches, which shortens the wood fibers and lowers the strength of the recycled paper. Vegetable Inks: The ester bonds in natural vegetable oils readily saponify (break down) in the mild alkaline wash solutions used in standard recycling plants. The detached ink particles bind naturally to injected air bubbles, floating cleanly to the surface to be skimmed off. This yields brighter, higher-purity recycled pulp with minimal fiber loss. 3. Comparative Analysis: Vegetable-Based vs. Petroleum-Based vs. Water-Based Inks Selecting the correct ink system depends on the printing process (sheetfed offset vs. flexographic vs. digital) and the target paperboard substrate. The comparison table below highlights the performance metrics across all three primary packaging ink systems. Performance Metric Vegetable-Based Inks Petroleum-Based Inks Water-Based Inks Primary Printing Process Sheetfed Offset / Litho-Lamination High-Speed Commercial Offset Flexographic / Corrugated Printing Carrier Vehicle Chemistry Soy, Linseed, Canola, or Tung Oils Mineral Distillates / Petroleum Solvents Water & Water-Soluble Acrylic Resins Average VOC Emissions Low ($15 - 60\text{ g/L}$) High ($250 - 350\text{ g/L}$) Ultra-Low ($0 - 20\text{ g/L}$) Drying Mechanism Oxidation & Paperboard Absorption Fast Evaporative Flash-Off & Heat Evaporation & Forced Air/Heat Tunnels Optical Density & Vibrancy Very High (Clear, translucent base) Moderate (Duller, yellowish base) Good (Dependent on pigment dispersion) De-Inking & Repulpability Excellent (Clean flotation detachment) Poor (Requires aggressive bleaches) Moderate (Water-soluble inks can stain wash) Substrate Compatibility Coated SBS, Uncoated Kraft, Rigid Board Non-Porous Plastics, Coated Boards Corrugated Flute, Kraft Paperboard Raw Material Cost Volatility Low (Tied to agricultural crop yields) High (Tracks crude oil market spikes) Stable (Regulated water/acrylic markets) 4. Top-Performing Brands: Real-World Industry Benchmarks Enterprise brand owners and high-volume commercial printers are leveraging vegetable ink formulations to meet sustainability metrics while enhancing unboxing presentation. INDUSTRY BENCHMARK LEADERS SUSTAINABLE PRINTING CO. APPLE INC. LUSH COSMETICS +------------------------+ +------------------------+ +------------------------+ | 100% vegetable oil | | Soy/vegetable inks | | Soy-based inks on 100% | | offset formulas for | | paired with protective | | post-consumer recycled | | zero-odor retail boxes | | aqueous (AQ) overprints| | shipping mailers | +------------------------+ +------------------------+ +------------------------+ Sustainable Printing Co. & Commercial Packaging Converters Leading commercial box manufacturers have made vegetable-based inks their default baseline for all litho-laminated corrugated mailers and folding cartons. By marketing $100\%$ vegetable oil formulations, these converters guarantee that retail client boxes arrive with zero chemical off-gassing, allowing D2C brands to promote verified eco-credentials right on the packaging dieline. Apple: Zero-Petroleum Ink Standard Apple eliminated petroleum-based inks across its global product packaging footprint. Every iPhone, Mac, and Apple Watch box is printed using soy and vegetable-based inks. To maintain high-speed press throughput and protect against scuffing during transit, Apple pairs these bio-based inks with water-based overprint varnishes, ensuring the packaging remains $100\%$ recyclable and repulpable. Lush Cosmetics: Uncoated Kraft Perfection Lush Cosmetics utilizes vegetable-based inks across its entire line of $100\%$ post-consumer recycled corrugated shippers and gift boxes. Because raw recycled Kraft paperboard is highly porous, petroleum inks tend to bleed and dull down. Lush leverages the high pigment density and translucent clarity of vegetable inks to achieve punchy, multi-color branding without compromising their closed-loop zero-waste policy. 5. 5-Step Pressroom & Procurement Framework: How to Transition Custom Box Printing Switching your custom box manufacturing from conventional petroleum inks to vegetable-based formulations requires managing press mechanics—specifically around setting speeds and inline drying. Follow this 5-step framework to ensure a smooth transition with zero press downtime or quality issues. 5-STEP IMPLEMENTATION WORKFLOW STEP 1: Audit Paperboard Substrate Compatibility [Match porous SBS, CRB, or Kraft stock to oxidative inks] | v STEP 2: Specify SoySeal / Low-VOC Standards on POs [Mandate >= 20% soy content and VOCs under 60 g/L] | v STEP 3: Apply Inline Aqueous (AQ) Sealing Coatings [Seal wet oxidative inks with water-based overprint coating] | v STEP 4: Require Low-Migration Certification for Sensitive Goods [Verify FDA 21 CFR or EU 1935/2004 food-contact compliance] | v STEP 5: Conduct Odor Audits & Archive MSDS Proofs [Audit off-gassing upon unboxing and store documentation for ESG] Step 1: Audit Paperboard Substrates & Press Compatibility Vegetable-based inks set through a combination of paperboard absorption and atmospheric cross-linking oxidation. Verify that your target substrates—whether Solid Bleached Sulfate (SBS), Clay-Coated News Back (CCNB), or uncoated Kraft corrugated—possess the necessary porosity to absorb the initial oil vehicle during the setting phase. Step 2: Specify Low-VOC Vegetable Ink Standards on Purchase Orders When issuing RFQs and Purchase Orders to custom box manufacturers, explicitly define your ink standards instead of asking for generic "eco-friendly ink": PURCHASE ORDER MANDATE SPECIFICATION "All offset litho-printing must utilize vegetable-based inks containing a minimum of 20% bio-based soy oil vehicle by weight (conforming to ASA SoySeal standards). Total VOC content must not exceed 60 g/L. Supplier must submit Technical Data Sheets (TDS) prior to press run." Step 3: Solve the Drying Speed Trade-Off with Inline Aqueous Coatings Because vegetable oil dries via slow oxidative cross-linking rather than fast solvent evaporation, un-coated vegetable inks take longer to fully cure. If stacked too quickly on pallets, wet ink can transfer onto the back of adjacent sheets (known as ink set-off ). INLINE AQUEOUS (AQ) SEALING LAYER +-------------------------------------------------+ | WATER-BASED AQUEOUS (AQ) OVERPRINT COATING | <-- Seals Surface Instantly +-------------------------------------------------+ | VEGETABLE INK LAYER (Dries via Oxidation Under) | <-- High Optical Saturation +-------------------------------------------------+ | PAPERBOARD SUBSTRATE (SBS / Kraft / CRB) | <-- Absorbs Carrier Oil +-------------------------------------------------+ The Solution: Apply a water-based inline aqueous (AQ) coating (matte, satin, or gloss) directly on press over the wet vegetable ink. The AQ coating dries instantly under infrared (IR) press lamps, creating a protective barrier that seals the ink layer. This allows sheets to be die-cut, folded, and glued immediately without waiting 24 hours for complete oxidation. Step 4: Require Low-Migration Certification for Food & Cosmetic Boxes If your custom packaging houses food items, skincare products, or pharmaceuticals, require your printer to provide proof of compliance with: FDA 21 CFR Part 175/178 (Indirect food contact compliance). EU Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 (Materials intended to come into contact with food). Nestlé Guidance Note on Packaging Inks (Strict low-migration standard). Step 5: Conduct Unboxing Odor Audits & Archive ESG Proofs Upon receiving mass production samples, perform a simple unboxing odor audit: seal three finished boxes in a room-temperature chamber for 24 hours, then open them to confirm the complete absence of solvent off-gassing. Save all supplier Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) and ink TDS documents in your central ESG archive to back up your brand's public sustainability claims. 6. Strategic Advice & Summary Transitioning custom box printing to vegetable-based inks provides a clear operational win: it pairs rich optical saturation and high-grade aesthetics with low VOC emissions and superior paperboard repulpability. While bio-based inks require careful press management regarding oxidative drying, pairing them with inline aqueous coatings eliminates pressroom bottlenecks and delivers press-ready boxes in standard turnaround windows. Furthermore, because vegetable oils are sourced from renewable agricultural crops rather than finite petrochemical reserves, their raw material pricing remains far more stable over long manufacturing cycles—decoupling your packaging costs from volatile crude oil spikes. Ready to upgrade your custom packaging to sustainable, low-VOC vegetable inks? title: Log Safety Events, Not Full Transcripts: One Audit Trade-Off
author: Basavaraj SH
summary: The FTC's inquiry into consumer AI products has turned a question most teams deferred into a launch requirement: can you show what your product actually did? That answer depends on a logging decision you make before launch - and can't retroactively fix. Content vs. Event Teams face two extremes. Keep every conversation, or keep nothing. Full transcripts answer any future question, which is exactly why they're expensive. Every retained message is breach surface, subpoena surface, and a trust cost you pay in your privacy policy. Teams that choose this path often discover their retention window was set by whoever wrote the database schema, not by anyone who thought about risk. Keeping nothing is cheap and genuinely privacy-protective - until someone asks how often your assistant encountered a user in distress and what it said back. You can't answer. Not "we'd rather not" - you structurally cannot, and neither can your own safety team, which means you also can't tell whether last month's guardrail change helped. The third option is to log the decision rather than the content. For each turn, write a structured event: which classifier fired (a classifier here is just a small model or rule that labels input, e.g. "self-harm mention" or "minor-related"), what action the system took, which policy and model version were live, a session hash. No raw user text. How do you tell which you need? Ask what question you'll be asked. Aggregate questions - how often, what did the system do, did the rate drop after the fix - are fully answered by event logs. Forensic questions - why did this specific conversation go wrong - need content. Most teams need the first continuously and the second rarely, which argues for event logs by default plus a small consented, access-controlled transcript sample. Real Example A minimal safety event, emitted alongside your normal request logs: { "session" : "sha256:9f2c..." , "ts" : "2025-11-18T14:03:22Z" , "flags" : [ "self_harm_mention" ], "action" : "crisis_resource_shown" , "policy_version" : "safety-2025.11.1" , "model" : "chat-v4.2" , "transcript_retained" : false } Six fields, no user content. From a month of these you can report: how many sessions triggered the flag, what percentage received the intended response, and whether that percentage improved after safety-2025.11.1 shipped. That is the shape of a regulatory question. The honest limitation: if a journalist surfaces one bad conversation, these logs tell you the system classified it and what it did - not what the user typed. That gap is the price. Decide consciously whether you pay it, and whether a 1% sampled transcript set with clear user disclosure closes it well enough. Key Takeaways Event-level safety logging answers aggregate accountability questions at a fraction of the privacy exposure of full transcript retention - the two are not equally risky. Pick based on the question you expect: rates and trends need events; single-conversation forensics needs sampled content, with disclosure and tight access control. Logging is not backfillable. Whatever you don't capture before launch is gone from your first safety review. If a regulator asked tomorrow how your product handled distressed users last quarter, which fields in your current logs would actually answer it? Sources referenced: HackerNews discussion on the FTC inquiry into OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies

title: Two-photo inputs beat a blank prompt: building Hotel Lobby AI with Next.js
author: zhifen zhu
summary: I built Hotel Lobby AI , a focused tool that turns two separate photos into an orange-booth rap duo video with generated audio. Here are a few implementation and interface decisions from a small Next.js, React, and TypeScript project. Give each upload a meaning Instead of one generic image picker, the interface asks for a left performer and a right performer. The implementation keeps two separate File values and two preview URLs. That makes the intended placement explicit before generation starts. The request also preserves the distinction: the multipart form has separate person1 and person2 fields, and the server validates both images. The useful idea is not the field names themselves; it is making the UI and request contract tell the same story. A preview has a lifecycle The photo previews use URL.createObjectURL . In a React component, replacing a selected file should also retire its old preview URL. Keeping preview state separate from output state helps avoid showing a generated result where the source photo is expected. For anyone building an upload-driven tool, I would check three states early: a new file selection, a replacement selection, and a missing required file. Those small transitions are easy to overlook when most attention goes to the model call. Expose useful choices, keep the scene focused The user can choose duration, 480P or 720P quality, and portrait or landscape format. The prepared performance workflow removes the need to write a prompt or edit a timeline. This is intentionally a narrow creative tool, not an attempt to expose every possible model parameter. The output includes generated audio and can be downloaded. Faces may vary from the source photos, so clear input guidance and realistic expectations matter. People should use photos they have permission to use. Explain the trial before generation Google sign-in is required. New users receive 20 credits, enough for one 4-second 480P trial. Further generations use credits available through one-time purchases. I prefer stating those conditions directly instead of calling the entire service unlimited or completely free. You can try the workflow at https://hotel-lobby-ai.org . I would welcome feedback on the clarity of the two-photo inputs, or how you structure upload state in your own React projects.

title: J'ai audité mon propre site sur les 106 critères du RGAA : ce que l'outil trouve seul, et ce qu'il rate
author: Charly Duguey
summary: En bref : j'ai audité mon site sur les 106 critères du RGAA. 71 applicables, 71 conformes. Mais un script ne juge que 24 critères sur 106, et le chiffre ne vaut rien sans sa méthode. Le 14 septembre 2026, j'ai audité mon propre site WordPress (thème enfant Blocksy) sur les 106 critères du RGAA 4.1, le référentiel français construit sur WCAG 2.1. Résultat : 71 critères applicables, 71 conformes, 35 non applicables, soit 100 %. Le détail est dans ma déclaration d'accessibilité , avec ses limites. Ce que ce 100 % ne dit pas Aucun test avec un lecteur d'écran réel. Je me suis appuyé sur l'arbre d'accessibilité du navigateur, pas sur l'interprétation d'un lecteur. C'est un audit interne. Je suis l'auteur du site et de l'audit. 35 critères sont non applicables : le site n'a ni vidéo, ni son, ni cadre, ni CAPTCHA, ni document à télécharger. Un site client en aura, son taux sera plus dur à tenir. La méthode 20 pages : les 5 pages obligatoires, 12 pages représentatives, et 3 tirées au hasard parmi les 55 du plan du site (tirage reproductible). Outils : Chromium piloté par Playwright (1366 par 900 pixels, puis 320 pixels de large avec un zoom à 200 %), le validateur du W3C et deux scripts maison. Répartition : un script juge seul 24 critères, je tranche les 82 autres à la main à partir des preuves relevées. Le script mesure Il ne sait pas juger présence d'un texte alternatif si ce texte décrit vraiment l'image contraste, focus visible l'ordre de lecture intitulés de liens, titres, repères le comportement au lecteur d'écran zoom à 200 %, lecture à 320 px les messages de correction de saisie étiquettes de champs, lien d'évitement l'espacement du texte Un rapport à 100 % sur les 24 critères mesurés ne veut donc jamais dire « conforme ». C'est la logique de l' audit d'accessibilité RGAA que je propose : les critères mesurés par l'outil, puis la vérification à la main, avec un rapport priorisé. Quatre pièges de mesure focus() en boucle ment. Le style natif dépend de :focus-visible , inactif sur un focus programmatique. J'ai testé à la vraie touche Tab, sur 45 arrêts par page. La cascade CSS ne se déduit pas du fichier. Blocksy repose la couleur de bordure des champs par une variable après mes règles. Seuls les outils de développement disent quelle règle gagne. Le contraste se calcule sur des couches composées. Une pellicule blanche à 5 % sur du bleu nuit n'est pas du blanc : sans composition, mon outil annonçait 1:1 sur du texte lisible. Le cache sert des copies différentes. Deux visites d'affilée ne renvoyaient pas la même feuille de style. Je demande chaque page sous une adresse jamais mise en cache. Ce que l'audit a trouvé sur mon site Contraste (3.2, 3.3) : bordure des champs à 1,24:1, passée à 3,47:1 ; numéro des cartes de 3,81:1 à 5,34:1. Lien d'évitement (12.7) : il pointait vers une ancre inexistante. Menu (10.13) : le panneau s'ouvrait au survol et ne se refermait pas. La touche Échap le masque maintenant. Langue (8.7) : les messages d'erreur du formulaire s'affichaient en anglais. Structure (8.9, 9.3) : une fausse liste faite de sauts de ligne est devenue une vraie liste de description. Code (8.2) : zéro erreur au validateur du W3C, contre sept par page le matin même. À retenir Un script ne remplace pas l'audit : il en couvre moins d'un quart. Un taux ne se cite jamais sans les critères non applicables ni la réserve du lecteur d'écran. La collecte se rejoue à volonté, mais la grille porte des jugements humains. Si l'audit trouve des défauts comme ceux-ci sur un site, la mise en conformité RGAA consiste à les corriger un par un, puis à re-mesurer.

title: Why an API works in curl but fails at the browser preflight
author: Arthur031221
summary: I have seen a request work in curl and fail before the browser sends the same POST. The difference can be an OPTIONS preflight. The browser asks whether the origin, method, and request headers are allowed. If the server responds with 401 or omits one of the required headers, the application request never goes out. I built corswhy to inspect that exchange from a terminal. It takes the URL of the API, the page origin, the intended method, and names from the browser's Access-Control-Request-Headers field. It sends OPTIONS with those details and prints one row for each check. The command does not send the POST, request body, or credentials. Here is the command used in the local fixture: node bin/corswhy.js http://127.0.0.1:18765/auth \ --origin http://localhost:5173 \ --method POST \ --header authorization,content-type The failing endpoint returns 401 to OPTIONS. The report names the status failure first and suggests letting OPTIONS reach the CORS handler without authentication. The second endpoint answers with a 204 response and the required allowed origin and header names, so its report passes. The repository tests also assert that the server sees OPTIONS and never sees POST. There are a few details that matter when reading the output. A GET, HEAD, or POST with no unsafe request headers usually does not require a preflight. In that case corswhy sends nothing and says so. The header names passed with --header should be the names a browser includes in Access-Control-Request-Headers. If cookies will accompany the real cross origin request, use --credentials include ; the allowed origin must then match the page origin and the preflight must allow credentials. A green report is limited to the OPTIONS exchange. It does not test the actual response or browser cookie policy. It also does not model private network access, service workers, or extensions. This scope is useful when the observed failure is specifically the preflight, but it should not be read as a full browser verdict. The source, local fixture, and test suite are at https://github.com/Arthur031221/corswhy . I would like reports of preflight responses that the command explains incorrectly, with any private headers removed first.
